title: Om, and the silence after
hookLine: a bell fades, and a verse says the quiet after Om is a door
carry: Om, and the silence beyond it
tomorrow: what could a sneeze possibly have to do with the sacred?

cards: The last guest leaves, the door clicks, and the house rings with quiet. Or a call ends badly, and the room seems louder than before. The silence after a big sound can feel empty, or like too much.
Here's a smaller version. A bell is struck once. Bright, then softer, then a hum at the edge of hearing, then gone.
When, exactly, does it stop? The ear keeps reaching after it. The Vijnana Bhairava is interested in that edge.

teach.b: Some of Bhairava's practices are built from sound. In one, a person chants the sacred syllable, Om, and draws it out long. As the sound fades, the attention follows it to its end and rests in the silence it leaves.

In another, a person listens to a stringed instrument, one long note, and follows it as it trails away. The sound is the boat; the silence on the far side is where the practice lands. This isn't a stray idea.
Hindus have long treated Om as Brahman in sound, the whole of reality in one syllable.

teach.h: A, U, M, AND A SILENT FOURTH.
teach.b: The Mandukya Upanishad hears four parts in it: A, U, M, and a fourth with no letter and no sound at all, the quiet the syllable falls into, which it calls the deepest.

teach.h: THE FADING IS PART OF THE WORD.
teach.b: So when Om is chanted and then left to fade, the fading isn't failure, or the dull part before the next round. It's the fourth part of the word.

When the sound thins out and the attention stays awake anyway, there's a moment of open listening with nothing yet to hear. In the Vijnana Bhairava's telling, that's a door to what can't be described.
The same text that pointed to the gap between two breaths now points to the gap after a sound.
A different sense, the same move: follow the sacred sound all the way to its edge, and stay awake there.

how: Some meditators chant Om slowly and rest in the silence after it, and some use a bell, a drone or a stringed instrument, following the sound as it fades.

o: chanting a syllable louder each round to build power
playing music to drown out a busy, noisy mind
a sound followed to its end, into open silence

games.q: sound, followed to its end. tap the pairs.
p: Om's soundless quiet, beyond A, U, M

s: in this practice, chanting Om is all about getting the sound right
it cares at least as much about the silence the sound leaves, which the Mandukya counts as Om's fourth part.
the book has a practice built on a stringed instrument's long note
followed as it trails away, to the quiet on the far side.

games.q: at the end of a yoga class everyone chants one Om, and the teacher sits in silence after it. a friend whispers, 'why the awkward pause?' what do you say?
o: the quiet is part of Om: the Upanishad hears a soundless fourth after A, U, M.
it's just to let the room settle before people pack up.
it's so the teacher can hear who chanted off-key.
games.why: the Mandukya Upanishad hears A, U, M and a soundless fourth; the Vijnana Bhairava follows Om into that silence and rests there.

practice: If you can, hum one long, low note, and follow it as it fades into quiet; if not, listen for one sound in the room as it ends. Then stay awake in the silence that's left, listening with nothing to hear, until the next sound comes.

wordCard.voice: The Vijnana Bhairava: here, sound followed to its end, and the open listening that waits on the far side.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Om, the sacred syllable, also called pranava; here chanted long and followed into silence.
